Section. Rules and Derivations Explanation. Natural deduction systems are meant to closely parallel the informal reasoning used in mathematical proof (hence it is somewhat “natural”). Natural deduction proofs begin with assumptions. Inference rules are then applied. Assumptions are “discharged” by the negation introduction, conditional introduction, disjunction elimination and existential quantifier elimination inference rules, and the label of the discharged assumption is placed beside the inference for clarity. Definition 1: Assumption. An assumption is any sentence in the topmost position of any branch. Derivations in natural deduction are certain trees of sentences, where the topmost sentences are assumptions, and if a sentence stands below one, two, or three other sequents, it must follow correctly by a rule of inference. The sentences at the top of the inference are called the premises, and the sentence below is called the conclusion of the inference. Reader correction: the source omits “is called” in the second clause. The rules come in pairs, an introduction and an elimination rule for each logical operator. They introduce a logical operator in the conclusion or remove a logical operator from a premise of the rule. Some of the rules allow an assumption of a certain type to be discharged. To indicate which assumption is discharged by which inference, we also assign labels to both the assumption and the inference. This is indicated by writing the assumption as “ assumption A, labeled n for discharge .” It is customary to consider rules for all the logical operators conjunction, disjunction, conditional, negation, and a contradiction, even if some of those are defined.

listen_text: Section. Derivations Explanation. We've said what an assumption is, and we've given the rules of inference. Derivations in natural deduction are inductively generated from these: each derivation either is an assumption on its own, or consists of one, two, or three derivations followed by a correct inference. Definition 9: Derivation. A derivation of a sentence formula A from assumptions Gamma is a finite tree of sentences satisfying the following conditions: Item 1. The topmost sentences of the tree are either in Gamma or are discharged by an inference in the tree. Item 2. The bottommost sentence of the tree is formula A. Item 3. Every sentence in the tree except the sentence formula A at the bottom is a premise of a correct application of an inference rule whose conclusion stands directly below that sentence in the tree. We then say that formula A is the conclusion of the derivation and Gamma its undischarged assumptions. If a derivation of formula A from Gamma exists, we say that formula A is derivable from Gamma, or in symbols: Gamma syntactically derives A. If there is a derivation of formula A in which every assumption is discharged, we write A is derivable without undischarged assumptions. Example 1. Every assumption on its own is a derivation. So, e.g., formula A by itself is a derivation, and so is formula B by itself. We can obtain a new derivation from these by applying, say, the conjunction introduction rule, Step 1 states formula A as a premise. Step 2 states formula B as a premise. Step 3 applies the conjunction introduction rule to 1, 2 and concludes A and B. The final conclusion is A and B. A and B These rules are meant to be general: we can replace the formula A and formula B in it with any sentences, e.g., by formula C and formula D. Then the conclusion would be C and D, and so Step 1 states formula C as a premise. Step 2 states formula D as a premise. Step 3 applies the conjunction introduction rule to 1, 2 and concludes C and D. The final conclusion is C and D. listen_text: Section. Proof-Theoretic Notions Editorial note. This section collects the definitions of the provability relation and consistency for natural deduction. Reader correction: the source omits “of” in this phrase. Explanation. Just as we've defined a number of important semantic notions (validity, entailment, satisfiability), we now define corresponding proof-theoretic notions. These are not defined by appeal to satisfaction of sentences in structures, but by appeal to the derivability or non-derivability of certain sentences from others. It was an important discovery that these notions coincide. That they do is the content of the soundness and completeness theorems. Definition 10: Theorems. A sentence formula A is a theorem if there is a derivation of formula A in natural deduction in which all assumptions are discharged. We write A is derivable without undischarged assumptions if formula A is a theorem and A is not derivable without undischarged assumptions if it is not. Definition 11: Derivability. A Sentence formula A is derivable from a set of sentences Gamma, Gamma syntactically derives A, if there is a derivation with conclusion formula A and in which every assumption is either discharged or is in Gamma. If formula A is not derivable from Gamma we write Gamma does not syntactically derive A. Definition 12: Consistency. A set of sentences Gamma is inconsistent if and only if Gamma syntactically derives a contradiction. If Gamma is not inconsistent, i.e., if Gamma does not syntactically derive a contradiction, we say it is consistent. Proposition 1: Reflexivity. If A is a member of Gamma, then Gamma syntactically derives A. Proof. The assumption formula A by itself is a derivation of formula A where every undischarged assumption (i.e., formula A ) is in Gamma. Proposition 2: Monotonicity. If Gamma is a subset of capital Delta and Gamma syntactically derives A, then capital Delta syntactically derives A. Proof. Any derivation of formula A from Gamma is also a derivation of formula A from capital Delta. Proposition 3: Transitivity. If Gamma syntactically derives A and A together with capital Delta syntactically derives B, then the combined assumptions Gamma and capital Delta syntactically derive B. Proof. If Gamma syntactically derives A, there is a derivation delta zero of formula A with all undischarged assumptions in Gamma. If A together with capital Delta syntactically derives B, then there is a derivation delta one of formula B with all undischarged assumptions in the union of the singleton set containing A with capital Delta. Step 3 applies the subderivation to 1 and concludes formula B. Step 4 applies the conditional introduction rule to 3 and concludes if A, then B. Step 5 states Gamma as a premise. Step 6 labels the subderivation derivation delta zero. Step 7 applies the subderivation to 5 and concludes formula A. Step 8 applies the conditional elimination rule to 4, 7 and concludes formula B. The final conclusion is formula B. Soundness is thus a kind of guaranteed safety property for derivation systems. Depending on which proof theoretic property is in question, we would like to know for instance, that Item 1. every derivable sentence is valid; Item 2. if a sentence is derivable from some others, it is also a consequence of them; Item 3. if a set of sentences is inconsistent, it is unsatisfiable.
